The base verb is inherited from Old Norse ríða (“to ride”), from Proto-Germanic *rīdaną (“to ride”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hreydʰ- (“to set in motion, ride”), likely a suffixed form of *h₃reyH- (“to move, churn”).

13448.etyen:
Modelled on Late Latin ēvangelicus (“evangelical”), itself from Ancient Greek εὐαγγελικός (euangelikós, “evangelical”). Synchronically, it can be analysed as evangelium (“gospel”) + -isk, using the learned stem evangel-, literally “of or relating to the gospel”.
The Greek adjective is built on εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news, gospel”) with -ικός (-ikós, “-ic, -ical”). Its εὐ- (eu-, “good, well”) element continues Proto-Hellenic *ehu- (“good”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁su- (“good”); the deeper origin of the ἄγγελος (ángelos, “messenger”) element is uncertain.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk eva

59528.etyen:
Compound of tabu (“taboo”) + ord (“word”), literally “taboo word”.
The first element, tabu (“taboo”), was borrowed through English taboo, ultimately from a Polynesian language; Store norske leksikon identifies Tongan tapu (“sacred, forbidden”) or Fijian tabu (“sacred, forbidden”) as the source. The second element, ord (“word”), is inherited from Old Norse orð (“word”), from Proto-Germanic *wurdą (“word, speech”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥dʰom (“word”).
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk tabuord, Danish tabuord, Swedish tabuord and German Tabuwort (“taboo word”).

1416.etyen:
First attested in 1750.
Borrowed from German also (“so, therefore; that is”), from Middle High German alsō (“so, thus”), from Old High German alsō (“completely so; exactly so”), from Proto-West Germanic *allswā (“completely so; exactly so, likewise”). The Proto-West Germanic form is composed of *all (“all, entirely”) and *swā (“so, thus”). The Norwegian form was influenced by alt (“all; entirely”).
Compare Danish altså (“so, therefore”), Norwegian Nynorsk altså and altso, Swedish alltså, Dutch alzo (“thus, so”) and English also.

1000072.etyen:
Either a Norwegian form of Magdalene or a short form of Amalie.
In the first analysis, the name belongs to the same Norwegian name family as Malene and Malin, ultimately continuing Ancient Greek Μαγδαληνή (Magdalēnḗ, “woman from Magdala”), the byname of Mary Magdalene, from Μαγδαλά (Magdalá, “Magdala”). The Norwegian form developed through the considerable shortening and adaptation characteristic of traditional Scandinavian forms of the name.
In the second analysis, Mali is a shortened form of Amalie. The latter is a Norwegian form of the Latinized Germanic name Amalia, ultimately based on Ger
